veranderings.rede: The preposition meaning 'after' takes the accent, as the lesson itself writes 'Ná die ete' later.
'Na iemand vernoem' is the Afrikaans idiom for 'named after'; 'na iemand genoem' calques English.
A future seen from the past takes 'sou' in a past-tense narrative, matching 'die naam sou kies' in the previous sentence.
Lifting and holding a baby up is 'hoog ophou'; 'hoog hou' is unidiomatic here.

veranderings.voor: Haar naam was Zanele en sy was
veranderings.na: Haar naam was Zanele, en sy was
veranderings.rede: AWS comma before 'en' joining two clauses that each have their own subject and verb.

veranderings.voor: liefgehê word.” „In ons familie kies Ouma die eerste naam.
veranderings.na: liefgehê word. In ons familie kies Ouma die eerste naam.
veranderings.rede: Closing and reopening the quotation with no speaker between makes it read as a second speaker; it is all Zanele's speech, so it should be one quotation (protected wording left intact).
'Bekommerd voel' echoes English 'felt worried'; 'was bekommerd' is the natural Afrikaans.

veranderings.na: die foto by tannie Elsa geneem
veranderings.rede: With Ouma Nomsa as subject, 'by haar' can be read as herself; naming tannie Elsa makes clear whose photo it was, as in the earlier 'die baba by tannie Elsa geneem'.

veranderings.na: Mila het dit nog altyd geweet
veranderings.rede: 'Nog altyd' is the Afrikaans for 'had always known' up to that moment; bare 'altyd' reads as habitual.
'Een ... op 'n slag' calques 'one at a time'; 'reël vir reël' is the natural Afrikaans.

vlae.teks: Mila was twaalf jaar oud en vir die eerste keer in haar lewe 'n niggie.
vlae.rede: Grammatical but easy to misread: 'niggie' means both niece and cousin, and saying Mila 'was' a niggie for the first time is unusual. 'Het vir die eerste keer 'n niggie gekry' would read more naturally, but it changes the meaning slightly (a first female cousin, not her first cousin at all), so a writer should decide which is meant.
